solver_candidate_counterexample: Take d=r=1. For any proposed uniform bound B, choose the admissible odd integer n=2B+13. Then no Laurent polynomial C_{1,1,n}(X,q) supported in X-degrees between -B and B can satisfy the required telescoping identities.
solver_summary:
Take the admissible pair d=r=1. I claim the asserted uniform bound B cannot exist. Assume for contradiction that such a B exists. Then for every odd n>1 there is a Laurent polynomial C(X)=C_{1,1,n}(X,q)=sum_{j=-B}^B c_j(q) X^j satisfying the telescoping identities. Choose the admissible odd integer n=2B+13.

For 1<=k<=n-1 the statement gives T_k = T_k C(q^k) - T_{k+1} C(q^{k+1}), where
T_k = [3k+1]_q (q,q,q;q^2)_k (q;q)_k^2 q^{-k(k+1)/2} / (q^2;q^2)_k.
Since q is an indeterminate, every factor of T_k is nonzero in Q(q), so T_k != 0 and we may divide by it. Computing the ratio gives
T_{k+1}/T_k = q^{-k-1} * (1-q^{2k+1})^3 * (1-q^{k+1})^2 * (1-q^{3k+4}) / ((1-q^{2k+2})(1-q^{3k+1})).
With X=q^k this is
R(X) = q^{-1} X^{-1} (1-qX^2)^3 (1-qX)^2 (1-q^4 X^3) / ((1-q^2 X^2)(1-qX^3)).
Hence for every k=1,...,n-1,
C(q^k) - R(q^k) C(q^{k+1}) = 1.
Therefore the expression
E(X) := (1-q^2 X^2)(1-qX^3) C(X) - q^{-1} X^{-1} (1-qX^2)^3 (1-qX)^2 (1-q^4 X^3) C(qX) - (1-q^2 X^2)(1-qX^3)
vanishes at X=q^k for k=1,...,n-1. Now P(X):=X^{B+1}E(X) is an ordinary polynomial in Q(q)[X]. Its degree is at most 2B+11: the middle term contributes at most degree (B+1)-1+11+B = 2B+11, and the other terms are smaller. But P(q),P(q^2),...,P(q^{n-1}) all vanish, and these are 2B+12 distinct roots because n-1=2B+12 and q is transcendental. A nonzero polynomial of degree at most 2B+11 over the field Q(q) cannot have that many roots, so P(X)=0. Thus E(X)=0 identically as a Laurent-polynomial identity.

Write C(X)=sum_{j=L}^U a_j X^j with a_L,a_U nonzero. In the identity E(X)=0, the first term has lowest X-exponent L, while the second term has lowest X-exponent L-1 (coming from the factor q^{-1}X^{-1} and the constant terms of the other factors). The rightmost term has lowest exponent 0. If L<=0, then E(X) would contain a negative-power term X^{L-1}, impossible. If L>=2, then the left-hand side would have no constant term, but the rightmost term contributes constant term -1, again impossible. Hence L=1. On the other hand, the first term has highest exponent U+5, whereas the second term has highest exponent U+10; its coefficient there is -q^{U+8} a_U, which is nonzero. Since the remaining term has degree 5, there is nothing that can cancel X^{U+10}. Contradiction.

So for d=r=1 no uniform B can satisfy the lemma. Hence the lemma statement is false.
